[JOHN-MCCON] [fades in] And then the ambassador says, """"""""This doesn't depend on us.""""""""� And [Mikhail] Suslov says, """"""""There will be instructions.""""""""� And the ambassador comes and says, """"""""That's good,""""""""� but he says, """"""""this doesn't depend upon us,""""""""� meaning, I guess, the Cubans. And the conversation ended by Suslov saying, """"""""All right, the instructions are coming, and wait.""""""""� So apparently, the Soviets took--were giving the ambassador instructions to prevent [unclear]{Note: [note 6] For the first two minutes of recording the volume is low.}--

[MCGEORGE-B] Or else they're telling you or giving you a message.{Note: [note 7] Bundy was alluding to the possibility that Soviet officials had used an open line (rather than more secure military or diplomatic lines) in the expectation that Western intelligence would monitor the conversation.}

[JOHN-MCCON] Or they might be giving us a message, yeah.

[DEAN-RUSK-] Yes, there was one interlude there that [unclear]-- Mr. President, I have a comment, a report from Jack McCloy on his talk with [Vasily] Kuznetsov at 4:00 this afternoon.{Note: [note 8] John J. McCloy was the chairman of the Coordinating Committee set up to negotiate with the Soviets on a settlement to the Cuban crisis. Vasily Kuznetsov was the Soviet first deputy minister of foreign affairs. After his meeting with Kuznetsov, McCloy had telephoned Rusk to report on the discussion. Later that evening, in a telegram signed by Stevenson, the U.S. Mission to the United Nations sent a formal report of this conversation to Washington. """"""""Telegram from the Mission to the United Nations to the Department of State,""""""""� 31 October 1962, in FRUS, 1961""""""""""""1963, 11: doc. 129.} After the usual amenities, Kuznetsov said that he was prepared to stay until the problem, this Cuba problem, was over. He hoped it would be as short a time as possible. McCloy emphasized that unless the U.N. was prepared to conduct aerial surveillance here during this period, that the U.S. would have to do it. Kuznetsov said that they [the Soviets] were proceeding rapidly with dismantling. It will only take a short time, but that on-site inspection could only occur after the dismantling had been completed. That the amount of time for the removal of this equipment will depend on the American quarantine, because obviously they can't bring their ship[s] in to take the stuff out, faced with the American quarantine. He then said that there were a number of problems that ought to be discussed. He didn't detail them, but he referred to messages that had been exchanged with the President and the Prime Minister.{Note: [note 9] This is a reference to British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan. At this point the volume of the recording increases sharply.}

[JOHN-KENNE] The Chairman?

[DEAN-RUSK-] The Chairman--no.

[JOHN-KENNE] The President and the Chairman?

[DEAN-RUSK-] No, no. Between the Chairman, and the President, and the Prime Minister. It implied that they were talking about Britain, but I have to double-check that [unclear].{Note: [note 10] There is clearly some confusion about which messages Kuznetsov mentioned. Possibly as a result of a query from the State Department, by the time Stevenson sent a written report of the McCloy- Kuznetsov meeting later that night, this confusion had been cleared up and the report referred only to the Kennedy-Khrushchev exchange.}

[JOHN-KENNE] [Unclear] to matter . . . he [Macmillan] did send a message. I don't know how he could--I don't remember what it was that Macmillan said to the Chairman, but it was something.

[MCGEORGE-B] Macmillan sent a message saying that your proposals were very sensible, which arrived just as the Soviet acceptance was going out on the wire.{Note: [note 11] In his 28 October message to Khrushchev, released publicly, British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan suggested that the settlement of the Cuban Missile Crisis could allow further progress on arms control, including a test- ban agreement. President Kennedy's message to Khrushchev had also referred to the prospects for arms control. By """"""""going out on the wire,""""""""� Bundy was referring to the broadcast of Khrushchev's decision to remove the missiles being broadcast on Radio Moscow. Telegram, Foreign Office to Moscow, 28 October 1962, FO 371/162384, The National Archives (United Kingdom); """"""""Telegram from the Department of State to the Embassy in the Soviet Union,""""""""� 28 October 1962, in FRUS, 1961""""""""""""1963, 11: doc. 104.}

[DEAN-RUSK-] Now, Kuznetsov emphasized the no-invasion point; this would be not only from here, but from all the Latin American countries. He referred to subversive groups. McCloy put back to him the point that this cuts both ways, that the whole problem in the whole Castro episode [unclear] Communist subversion against other countries and that this is not something that just can be dealt with on a unilateral basis. Kuznetsov asked [Anastas] Mikoyan--asked McCloy to come to dinner with them tomorrow night. And Mikoyan--McCloy held that open.{Note: [note 12] Rusk does not make himself clear on this point, apparently correcting himself at several points. The corresponding passage from the written account of the meeting reads: """"""""At one point early in [the] conversation Kuznetsov said Mikoyan [was] arriving [in] N[ew] Y[ork at] 2[:00] or 3[:00] P.M. [on] Nov[ember] 1 and leaving N[ew] Y[ork] shortly after noon [on] Nov[ember] 2. Mikoyan would like [to] meet with McCloy and extended [an] invitation to dinner [on] Nov[ember] 1. McCloy said he would of course make himself available for meeting with Mikoyan, but [was] not quite sure whether he had any prior engagement for tomorrow night.""""""""� """"""""Telegram from the Mission to the United Nations to the Department of State,""""""""� 31 October 1962, in FRUS, 1961""""""""""""1963, 11: doc. 129.} We'll see what we're going to have. McCloy did say that we are going to have to have surveillance tomorrow, whereupon Kuznetsov said, """"""""Well, you know, we don't have Russians manning antiaircraft; this is in the hands of the Cubans.""""""""� When McCloy mentioned the difficulties that they were having with Castro and indicated that it would be very strange if we and the Russians had to get together to try and deal with Castro, Kuznetsov just laughed.{Note: [note 13] The written account of the meeting reads: """"""""McCloy expressed hope Castro would be less recalcitrant and observed U.S. and Sov[iet]s might find themselves united vis-a�-vis Castro. Kuznetsov smiled.""""""""� """"""""Telegram from the Mission to the United Nations to the Department of State,""""""""� 31 October 1962, in FRUS, 1961""""""""""""1963, 11: doc. 129.} There was no mention of Guantanamo.

[JOHN-KENNE] Can I say, it seems to me that with [Yuri] Zhukov in town and Kuznetsov having conversations with various people--with Stevenson, McCloy, and different--what we ought to do is not have any conversation about any matter except Cuba until Cuba is straightened out.{Note: [note 14] Yuri Zhukov, the foreign editor of Pravada, was visiting Washington for meetings with journalists and government officials.} They'll try to get us involved in all these other matters, and then, when we're not forthcoming . . . that sort of--and so I think if we just say to them, tell everybody in the government to say to them, """"""""We'll be glad to have you stay around. We'll be glad to go into it, as soon as we get this thing worked out. We can do it just very quickly, as you said. We'd be glad, then, to open up the whole spectrum.""""""""� But, I think . . . otherwise, we've got this fellow seeing Walter Lippmann this afternoon, he's seeing somebody else, and they get all sorts of ideas, and pretty soon we get all of Berlin and about eight other things all mixed into Cuba.{Note: [note 15] Walter Lippmann was an influential columnist who wrote a regular column that was syndicated by the Washington Post and a weekly column that appeared in Newsweek. The President was especially sensitive to Lippmann's meetings with Soviet officials because Lippmann had demonstrated repeatedly that he was not afraid to put forward his own proposals for solutions to international problems. Indeed, Lippmann had already criticized the administration's decision to blockade Cuba rather than negotiate a trade of the Soviet missiles in Cuba for the American missiles in Turkey.} What is your judgment?

[DEAN-RUSK-] I think that is correct. And I think that's a--

[JOHN-KENNE] Couldn't we just say to this fellow, """"""""God, we're--let's get this out. Then we'll go into the whole other thing.""""""""� If you start getting--you sort of start talking about Berlin in the context of Cuba, the next thing we know they'll try to bring all these things into the deal. So I think we probably ought to just adopt a government policy of instructions and listen to any proposal they make. Say, """"""""We'd be delighted to discuss it. Let's get this matter cleaned up, then we'll go right ahead with these others.""""""""�

[DEAN-RUSK-] Well, Mr. President, General [Indar] Rikhye from Havana told New York that if we put in air surveillance tomorrow, that they would . . . it would get a warm reception. They were not able to work that out down there. {Note: [note 16] Brigadier General Indar Jit Rikhye, military adviser to Acting U.N. Secretary-General U Thant, was sending back reports from Havana to the United Nations in New York on the talks with Cuban leaders. Charles Yost, of the U.S. delegation to the United Nations, had conveyed Rikhye's warning that U.S. surveillance planes would get a """"""""warm reception""""""""� to McCloy and Stevenson at a midafternoon meeting in Stevenson's office. John McCloy Meeting Notes, 31 October 1962, in Folder 18, Box 1, Cuban Missile Crisis Series, John J. McCloy Papers, Amherst College.} Now, I think that that means that we ought to build up the pressures here. And I would urge that--

[MCGEORGE-B] What do you mean, """"""""a warm reception""""""""�? That they might fire?

[DEAN-RUSK-] Presumably, they'd be fired at. And Kuznetsov then tried to put this over on the Cubans by saying that antiaircraft down there is in Cuban hands. I don't--I didn't have a specific indication from McCloy, in my conversation, that he was including the SAM [surface-to-air missile] sites.{Note: [note 17] At this point the tape stops and repeats the previous few seconds as the reel switches over.} [to Robert McNamara] But you got that impression?

[ROBERT-MCN] I talked to Ros[well Gilpatric] just before coming over, and that was his definite understanding after having talked to McCloy, that Kuznetsov meant both the SAM sites and the field antiaircraft were in the hands of Cubans.{Note: [note 18] Roswell Gilpatric, who was deputy secretary of defense and a member of the Coordinating Committee, was in New York at the time.}

[JOHN-KENNE] [Unclear] SAM sites? [Unclear exchanges.]

[ROBERT-MCN] This is the impression Ros had.

[DEAN-RUSK-] Yeah.

[ROBERT-MCN] I think it extremely unlikely, and I think Kuznetsov might have simply been trying to create the impression so that if an incident occurs, that they can wash their hands of it.

[JOHN-KENNE] Of course, if you could--what is your--what could we get if we go on the presumption that the SAM sites are in the hands of the Russians? And if they've just gone in, it's very doubtful that the Cubans would be running the SAM sites.{Note: [note 19] U.S. intelligence estimated that about six months to a year of intensive, specialized training was required to man the SA-2 weapon system. Memorandum, CIA, """"""""Cuba 1962: Khrushchev's Miscalculated Risk,""""""""� 13 February 1964, Box 35, National Security File, Lyndon B. Johnson Library.}

[ROBERT-MCN] I don't believe they could.

[JOHN-KENNE] Then you could do the U-2 [flights] without--the question is whether the U-2 would give you the information.

[ROBERT-MCN] It would not. [Unclear interjection.] Particularly tomorrow, Mr. President. The weather is bad tomorrow, predicted to be bad, and therefore the U-2 flights will show very little. And under--

[JOHN-KENNE] [Unclear.] The question is whether we ought to just do the . . . the only place we got shot at before was the airfield.

[MAXWELL-TA] And that was on a second pass.

[JOHN-KENNE] Second pass. What about just doing the [missile] sites?

[ROBERT-MCN] I think the airfield is very important to us, because we don't know what's going on there, and the bombers fall in a somewhat ambiguous category.

[JOHN-KENNE] They've got time to make one pass, though, don't they?

[ROBERT-MCN] Yes, exactly.

[DEAN-RUSK-] I would think we ought to do it low level and not U-2 tomorrow.

[ROBERT-MCN] I would certainly agree.

[DEAN-RUSK-] So we don't--

[ROBERT-MCN] I believe General Taylor would also.

[DEAN-RUSK-] So we can throw this entirely on Cuban hands if we need to.

[JOHN-KENNE] Now, has anybody suggested that if we do this surveillance that this is going to break the . . . ? Is U Thant going to be able to . . . or anybody going to be able to make a speech saying that the fact that we did surveillance tomorrow, while--is he there, or is he coming back?

[DEAN-RUSK-] Oh, he's back. He'll be back about 8:30 tonight, at Idlewild.{Note: [note 20] Idlewild Airport was in Queens, in New York City. On 24 December 1963, it was rededicated as John F. Kennedy International Airport.} [Unclear.]

[JOHN-KENNE] Well, has anybody warned us that this is going to screw up the deck? We haven't got any such warnings from anybody, have we? Or any--

[DEAN-RUSK-] Well, he's had full warning that we expect to surveil except during the period he's actually there. [Pause.] [reading] """"""""The Secretary-General sent a personal message to the U.S. government requesting most earnestly that the U.S. refrain from any aerial reconnaissance over Cuba tomorrow, October 31.""""""""� That's today. """"""""The request is limited to this single day. The Secretary-General feels that this might have significant bearing on the results of these negotiations.""""""""� Mr. President, I think that we need to build up again some feeling of pressure from our side, and I would hope you would consider letting Pierre [Salinger] say that in view of the continued gravity of the Cuban crisis, the President has canceled his press conference.

[JOHN-KENNE] I have canceled already.

[DEAN-RUSK-] It's been done?

[JOHN-KENNE] Yeah, I just said """"""""until the situation is clarified.""""""""�

[DEAN-RUSK-] Right. Well, I think that's fine, because I think that that itself is a gesture of pressure on the other side that is very useful here. So that's [unclear].

[ROBERT-MCN] Mr. President, I'd recommend that we resume the quarantine at daybreak tomorrow, applying a simple hail procedure, which if responded to would lead to no search.{Note: [note 21] McNamara was referring to a procedure in which a ship approaching the blockade line would be hailed and asked about its cargo, port of origin, and destination. Provided the ship responded satisfactorily, it would be allowed to pass. This was a way to maintain the quarantine without risking unnecessary provocation of having U.S. personnel board and search Soviet ships.}

[JOHN-KENNE] Fine, good. Now, do we want to tell Kuznetsov this is what we're going to do?

[DEAN-RUSK-] I think we ought to tell him, yes.

[ROBERT-MCN] I think we should, definitely.

[JOHN-KENNE] Tonight?

[ROBERT-MCN] Yes.

[JOHN-KENNE] OK.

[ROBERT-MCN] Secondly--

[DEAN-RUSK-] Now, a hail procedure would involve . . . name, destination--

[ROBERT-MCN] Name, port of origin, port of destination, cargo. And in the event the reply was unsatisfactory, we would instruct the Navy to report that back here and I would get in touch with the secretary of state and yourself . . .

[JOHN-KENNE] OK. OK.

[ROBERT-MCN] . . . before any further--

[JOHN-KENNE] We'll tell him that tonight.

[DEAN-RUSK-] Right.

[JOHN-KENNE] And we'll tell him the surveillance tonight, or not?

[DEAN-RUSK-] Well, we've told them already about the surveillance.

[ROBERT-MCN] We've told them the surveillance.

[JOHN-KENNE] OK.

[ROBERT-MCN] I think the question on surveillance is, how much? The Defense Intelligence Agency and General [Curtis] LeMay and, I believe, General [Maxwell] Taylor believe we should carry on extensive surveillance of the sites, the ports, and the roads.{Note: [note 22] General Curtis LeMay was chief of staff of the Air Force. General Maxwell Taylor was chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.} In the past, the low-level strikes on the sites have given to us only a 750-foot- wide swath of intelligence.{Note: [note 23] By """"""""strikes,""""""""� McNamara was referring to photographic overflights, not armed action.} That's very narrow. They're moving the erectors out of that swath along the sides. To expand it to cover the territory on the edges of the swath would require 14 stories in place of 8. To cover the 2 primary ports excluding Havana would require 2 more sorties. To cover the important road complexes would require still 2 more, for a total, I believe, General Taylor would recommend, of 18. General LeMay recommends 30. I'd recommend 10 or 12.

[JOHN-KENNE] What about this? Can we get it so they make one pass?

[ROBERT-MCN] Yes.

[MAXWELL-TA] Yes, sir, we can do that.

[ROBERT-MCN] Yes, we can do that.

[JOHN-KENNE] All right, we . . . I think we can do this with 12.

[MAXWELL-TA] I think we have to ask ourselves what we expect from this reconnaissance [unclear], Mr. President. The photography of the sites can do nothing more than tell us someday [that] everything has gone. Conceivably, the photography of roads and ports can prove movement along the roads and, finally, into the port area. To do that we should start looking at the ports in particular now, where we haven't looked. If you consider that is not going to be worth the effort, then that's another matter. [Unclear.]

[JOHN-KENNE] What do you think about that?

[ROBERT-MCN] Well, I am a little uncertain as to the reception these planes will meet, and I think it would be quite unfortunate if we lost a plane. The chances of losing a plane increase as the number of planes increase.

[JOHN-KENNE] I was going to say, what is our . . . well, I think, why don't we do the--

[UNKNOWN-19] Fourteen.

[JOHN-KENNE] --whatever it was [unclear] look over this.

[ROBERT-MCN] Let's say 14.

[JOHN-KENNE] OK. And have them make just the one pass.

[ROBERT-MCN] All right, let's [unclear].

[JOHN-KENNE] Now--

[MCGEORGE-B] What is the process for announcement, Mr. President? Might as well pin that down. Will the Defense Department announce both the quarantine and the surveillance?

[JOHN-KENNE] I think we announce . . . [unclear]--

[PIERRE-SAL] I don't think we announce surveillance [unclear]--

[JOHN-KENNE] No, we announce the quarantine. We tell Kuznetsov privately the procedure we're going to follow. Now, do we announce in advance the procedure?

[DEAN-RUSK-] I wouldn't, no.

[ROBERT-MCN] I wouldn't.

[DEAN-RUSK-] I wouldn't suggest any public announcement on this.

[PIERRE-SAL] Just describe--just make a simple statement at the end of the meeting that the quarantine will be reinstituted at daybreak tomorrow. Period.

[ROBERT-MCN] Yeah.

[JOHN-KENNE] Well, not at the end of the meeting, when we've told Kuznetsov. Then let's put it out later tonight.

[DEAN-RUSK-] Mr. President, I would like to--

[MCGEORGE-B] [Unclear] get it out on the wire then. [Unclear background exchange.]

[DEAN-RUSK-] I would like to hold up, if I may, until we get a direct report from U Thant as to his talks. He'll arrive later tonight.

[JOHN-KENNE] Yeah, all right. I'll tell you what, don't put it out until you've cleared the quarantine announcement with the secretary of state and the secretary of defense. Surveillance, we won't announce in any case, but we will let Kuznetsov know about it. Now, let me ask, what about this Voice of America? Did you get that memorandum from the British ambassador? {Note: [note 24] This memorandum has not been found.}

[DONALD-WIL] I did, sir, yes.

[JOHN-KENNE] Do you think there was much to that?

[DONALD-WIL] Well, I thought there was something to it, and we have another rather interesting one from the Canadians today. Do you want me to . . . ?

[JOHN-KENNE] No, but I just wanted you to . . . he said the shortwave stuff they don't have and a lot of other stuff is in English. Is he right there?

[DONALD-WIL] Well, there may be some English in the daytime coming through from a couple of isolated stations in Florida. The Canadian ambassador who reported in today has a much better picture than the [unclear].{Note: [note 25] The Canadian ambassador to Cuba was George Kidd. Because the United States did not have a diplomatic presence in Cuba, U.S. officials had previously asked officials at the Canadian embassy in Havana to supply information. See John Graham, """"""""Whose Man in Havana? Adventures on the Far Side of Diplomacy,""""""""� unpublished manuscript.}

[JOHN-KENNE] I'd like to look at that after. Now, the question is, what is the line we ought to be taking in our propaganda to Havana? We shouldn't be really attacking Castro this week with . . . particularly, I think, because as I [unclear]--

[DONALD-WIL] We're not attacking Castro this week.

[JOHN-KENNE] What are we saying? What's our line?

[DONALD-WIL] All right, sir, I'll give you the . . . I'll give it to you. These are the six main points that we've been making: The U.S. welcomes the agreement with Khrushchev and it spells it out in principle, but much remains to be done. And our tone so far has been very steady and a generally cautious one. That the removal of the Soviet offensive missile bases in Cuba is of primary importance at this time. That this has been a confrontation between the U.S. and Soviets. And we have played, but rather lightly, the role of Mr. Castro as a pawn of Khrushchev's.

[JOHN-KENNE] But I wouldn't play that.

[DONALD-WIL] Not hard at all.

[JOHN-KENNE] I wouldn't play that at all. I'd say, """"""""This is an OAS [Organization of American States] decision that there shouldn't be these weapons in the hemisphere.""""""""�

[DONALD-WIL] Well, that was my--my fourth point is that the American republics strongly support our position by word and deed. Five, that the Rio Treaty and other inter-American agreements are in full force, and our position is in line with such agreements. Six, that the U.S. looks forward, as indicated in President Kennedy's reply to Khrushchev, to urgent action on disarmament and nuclear test-ban negotiations. And we have avoided all speculation. And we have avoided denunciatory anti-Communist materials. We have avoided gloating. That's it.

[JOHN-KENNE] OK. I just wouldn't do the """"""""Castro is a pawn,""""""""� because that's going to be that . . .

[DONALD-WIL] All right, sir, we'll--

[JOHN-KENNE] This week, that seems to me [unclear].

[DONALD-WIL] We have been light on it.

[JOHN-KENNE] Then I would say, I would just emphasize that OAS [point]. That all the countries of the hemisphere made this judgment. This isn't the United States versus Russia or versus Cuba. It's all the countries in the OAS made the determination that these kinds of weapons should be kept out of the hemisphere. Then I'd like to take a look at the Canadian thing. And then I think we ought to try to keep in touch with these British and the Canadians and others and get their impression of our broadcasts as we go along, every three or four days if we could set that up.

[DONALD-WIL] We are doing it on a regular basis.

[JOHN-KENNE] [aside] OK. Could you let me see that? You go along, yeah?

[DEAN-RUSK-] [Unclear] brief report on that this morning. [Pause.]

[JOHN-KENNE] [Unclear.]

[DEAN-RUSK-] We have sent out the telegram to several other countries suggesting they call in the Cuban ambassador and say that if Cuba doesn't cooperate with the U.N. that they'll have to review their relations with Cuba. I think that kind of pressure, as long as we've been able to put it on, will be very helpful.{Note: [note 26] Telegram, Rusk to Missions, 31 October 1962, in FRUS, 1961""""""""""""1963, 11 (supplement): doc. 469.}

[JOHN-KENNE] Now, the other thing is, we arrested these people this afternoon going out to . . . [unclear] we arrested-- using the PT-109.{Note: [note 27] """"""""U.S. Seizes Ten Armed Cuba Exiles,""""""""� Washington Post, 1 November 1962.} Did you know that? [Laughter and unclear comments.]

[UNKNOWN-19] What?

[JOHN-KENNE] The PT that was being used for the film, the PT-109, was used{Note: [note 28] The movie PT-109, directed by Leslie Martinson, was released in theaters in June 1963.}--

[UNKNOWN-19] [Unclear] standing by?

[JOHN-KENNE] [Unclear] was standing by. It was used down in Florida to stop the--

[MCGEORGE-B] To catch Alpha 66?{Note: [note 29] Alpha 66 was another anti-Castro Cuban a�migra� force that conducted hit-and-run actions against Cuba.} [Unclear exchanges.]

[JOHN-KENNE] Why don't we--we ought to say this to Kuznetsov to indicate our good faith about these things, if he needs it, and certainly to U Thant. There ought to be a report to both of them. And I think, if it's possible, you know, I mean, Zhukov this afternoon said to Pierre [unclear]{Note: [note 30] Salinger's report on his conversation with Zhukov is: """"""""Memorandum from the President's Press Secretary (Salinger) to President Kennedy,""""""""� 31 October 1962, in FRUS, 1961""""""""""""1963, 5: doc. 258.}--

[DEAN-RUSK-] [Unclear.] That's all I have.

[MCGEORGE-B] May I get you one second, Mr. President, on another matter, which is whether we should sign off on the famous Dryden-Blagonravov agreement or hold it.{Note: [note 31] This agreement on """"""""peaceful uses of outer space""""""""� called for cooperation in three areas: meteorological satellites; satellites to map the earth's magnetic fields; and experiments in space communications. Negotiated in June 1962 by Hugh L. Dryden, the deputy administrator of NASA, and Anatoly A. Blagonravov of the Soviet Academy of Sciences, the agreement was formalized by an exchange of letters between Academy of Sciences President M. V. Keldysh and NASA Administrator James E. Webb on 18 and 30 October 1962 but was not formally announced until December 5, 1962 (http://www.hq.nasa.gov/office/pao/History/SP-4209/ch2- 3.htm). The text of the agreement and related documents are reprinted in the Department of State Bulletin 67 (1962): 962""""""""""""65.} They're all ready to put it into effect. The State Department--

[JOHN-KENNE] Space?

[MCGEORGE-B] This is the space cooperation agreement. The State Department told the Soviet Foreign Ministry it had no objections back in August. The Soviet Foreign Ministry answered in October, saying it had no objections. The president of the Soviet Academy wrote Jim Webb on October 12, saying they're ready to go. And Jim would like to write{Note: [note 32] In fact, Webb's letter had been written the previous day, but NASA was waiting for White House approval before sending it. Webb to Koldysh, 30 October 1962, in the Department of State Bulletin 67 (1962): 965.}--

[JOHN-KENNE] Well, I think if we--if the surveillance tomorrow shows they're not [unclear]--

[MCGEORGE-B] Hold it for a day or two. It might be a good play, later in the week.

[JOHN-KENNE] Then I think it might be. We ought to go ahead with that. I think we ought to review the air one [the civil air transport agreement], which was . . . was the air one initialed?{Note: [note 33] The civil air transport agreement, which provided for commercial air services between New York and Moscow, had been negotiated during the spring and summer of 1961 and initialed by Alexis Johnson and Yevgeni F. Loginov on 21 August 1961. However, for the following five years, the U.S. government delayed signing the agreement, in part because of concerns about rewarding the Soviet government despite continued East-West tensions. The agreement was finally signed and came into force on 4 November 1966. """"""""Civil Air Transport Agreement between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics,""""""""� 4 November 1966, in Department of State, United States Treaties and Other International Agreements (Washington, DC: GPO, 1967), vol. 17, pt. 2, no. 6135, pp. 1909""""""""""""18.}

[MCGEORGE-B] [Unclear.]

[JOHN-KENNE] All right, I thought that was initialed by [Charles] Bohlen.{Note: [note 34] Charles Bohlen was U.S. ambassador to the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1957 and was the newly installed U.S. ambassador to France.}

[LYNDON-JOH] Let's see, yes, that was initialed here. That was the air transport agreement.

[JOHN-KENNE] Why don't we check into that. Let's see how near that would be to signing.

[LYNDON-JOH] Oh, that's ready to go. That's ready to go.

[JOHN-KENNE] Why don't we review it in light of the present and see whether we want to do both if we make real progress on this thing, just as a . . .

[LYNDON-JOH] I should think [unclear] at the end of this period, you would--[Unclear exchanges.] I wouldn't think you'd want to do it until they--

[JOHN-KENNE] No. Why don't you take a look at it and see whether we ought to suggest that?

[DEAN-RUSK-] [Unclear] we get these missiles out of Cuba. This is the pathological concentration point.

To sum up Mr. President the most important judgments in this year's Estimate are: During the next ten years the Soviets almost certainly will not have a first-strike capability to prevent devastating retaliation by the United States. Short of this however Soviet strategic programs present what we believe are real and more proximate dangers to the United States -with or without a SALT TWO agreement. We think there will probably be a continuation of rough strategic equality between the U. S. and USSR but in the qualitative competition the U. S. technological lead will come under increasing challenge. Assuming that the judgments of the Estimate are reasonably correct I believe that foreseeable Soviet strategic forces would not eliminate. the USSR's vulnerability to retaliation. Consequently a crisis resolution probably would not rest on the strategic weapons balance but rather would depend on other factors such as the comparative strengths and dispositions of U. S. and Soviet conventional forces. It is relevant in this connection to note the steady increases occurring in Warsaw Pact forces opposite NATO and in the Soviet Navy. Let me now turn to the future of Soviet politics which could affect the Soviet strategic posture fully as much as force projections or progress in R&D. These future developments are best looked at in/:/ three stages: -At the present in the two months before the Party Congress Brezhnev still is the dominant Soviet leader. His authority seems to be in a slow decline along with his physical vigor. He is still interested in a SALT agreement but is clearly prepared to go into the Congress without one if necessary. He doubtless recognizes that both sides have to change their existing formal positions to reach a deal and he has some room for maneuver -though not we believe to the extent of agreeing to include Backfire in a 2 400 aggregate. -In the months after the Congress we will probably have roughly the same Soviet leadership and no major change in SALT policy. But the gradual erosion of Brezhnev's position will continue as his colleagues begin to cast their minds forward to the post-Brezhnev period. The further this process goes the more the individual Politburo members will be inclined to avoid risky decisions that might lay them open to attack at a later more intense phase of the succession competition. -Â More important in this period however will be Soviet concern about the uncertainties of the U. S. political process. They will be cautious about such hazards as negotiating during an election year when the whole Soviet American relations could be pushed into the forefront of partisan debate. We do not believe they will out-and-out refuse to continue discussions but they seem prepared to wait until 1977 if necessary. In the third phase over the next several years the Politburo will get deeply into what we expect to be a prolonged succession process. Real factional struggles might develop with none of the aspirants for power wanting to antagonize the military. Thus the preferences of the marshals will probably be given greater weight in strategic and arms control matters. Finally what can we say about the prospects for SovietU. S. relations if there is no SALT TWO? We believe Moscow sees this as primarily up to the Americans. The Soviets find detente too useful to want to repudiate it and would hope to continue on a pragmatic course governed by the opportunities and risks of specific situations and still call it detente. The chief consequences for Soviet foreign policy therefore of no SALT agreement would lie more in the area of underlying attitudes than in specific behavior on the international scene. Soviet uncertainty about the future strategic balance would encourage darker interpretations of U. S. intentions. If the strategic dialogue ended the beginnings of confidence-building would be interrupted. In the absence of treaty limitations the Soviet military would be relieved of the healthy necessity to dismantle older systems and to divulge strategic facts to their chief opponents. All this would clearly be damaging to the prospects for positive long-run change in the Soviet system. These effects would be magnified if the U. S. reaction to a SALT failure was to discredit detente altogether from the Western side.

I said then--this is in absolute confidence, any statement or any speeches or any comment at this time referring to the substance of this conversation will be injurious. I don't think there's any question about that and I know you would not want that to happen. First, our position--the government's position today--is exactly what it was the last time all three of you were briefed. That position mainly is this. We're anxious to stop the bombing and would be willing to stop the bombing if they--Hanoi--would sit down with us, with the Government of South Vietnam present, and have productive discussions. We have told them that we did not think that we could have productive discussions if, while we were talking, they were shelling the cities, or if they were abusing the DMZ. That was on October 16th, when I talked to you. The next sentence said, """"From time to time they have nibbled back and forth at these various items."""" Each time they do, there is a flurry of excitement, and so on and so forth. Since that time, they have sent their man back to Hanoi. We have continued to have our regular weekly meetings and other meetings. We have been in touch with a good many Governments in the world, from Eastern Europe to India to the Soviet Union, all these people working every hour to try to (a) get them to accept the Government of South Vietnam--that they're all puppets and that they'd never sit down in a room with, and (b) trying to inform them that we would be glad to stop the bombing, but that the bombing could not continue stopped if they (a) shelled the cities or (b) if they abused the DMZ. On Sunday3 night, I was informed by Paris that there were very good indications that they would let the Government of Vietnam come and be present at the conference and that they fully understood what would happen if we stop the bombing and they shell the cities or abuse the DMZ. When I got back to Washington from New York, I went back to the Soviet Union and pointed out that I did not want to deceive anybody and didn't want them to be deceived, didn't want to stop the bombing and have to start it again, but I wanted to make it abundantly clear that if they would let the Government of Vietnam come to the meetings and if they thoroughly understood what would happen, then I wanted to seriously consider this matter. But I had doubts--repeat doubts--that the North Vietnamese would stop shelling the cities or would stop abusing the DMZ. The Soviet Union came back to me on Tuesday or Wednesday and said that my doubts were not justified.4 Ambassador Harriman came back to me and said, """"We have repeated to you at least 12 times--we've repeated to North Vietnam at least 12 times--in 12 meetings, and some meetings we repeated it several times--that we could not have a productive discussion in an atmosphere of shelling the cities or abusing the DMZ. [RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Hm-hmm.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Let me describe some of the issues which we will face in the reassessment of a Middle East policy. First what have we been trying to achieve? If the situation had been allowed to continue given the economic problem in the West all the pressures would have been on us. And at Geneva everyone would have been united against Israel with the US acting as Israel's lawyer. Our policy helped abort this sort of Geneva Conference even though we went along with the idea in order to keep the Russians calmed down. We had the willingness of Sadat to play a constructive cooperative role and the active encouragement of Faisal for the step-by-step approach. This held off the radicals and enabled us to create a situation in which all the Arabs were turning to us while Israel had a situation which it could handle politically since it had to deal with only a small piece at a time. We also neutralized the Western Europeans and Japanese who are anxious to replace us in the Middle East. Objectively there is little to distinguish the effect of their policies from those of the Soviets. This process which we instituted proceeded well and met Israel's interests as well as our own. The two were compatible in the step-by-step approach. So the big issue with Israel during my last trip was not lines on maps. By the way the leaked maps in the New York Times and elsewhere are inaccurate. They only showed us a map after the negotiations were over. But lines are trivial compared to whether or not the moderate Arab leaders are able to say the US has delivered something. And this is fully in line with the survival of Israel really the best way to ensure Israel's survival. The USSR was completely out of the game and on this last trip Feisal came to the point where he told me he trusted me to proceed as I judged best even though he would have preferred another approach. And Asad told me he wanted separate negotiations with Israel rather than Geneva. So our disappointment is that Israel did not understand. They could have been shielded and their only friend literally their only friend in the world was in control of the process dealing with the Arabs singly and keeping the USSR out. Even Iraq was beginning to move out of the Kurdish orbit. I do not approve of the brutal way in which Iran and Iraq disposed of the fate of the Kurds but it created a situation whereby the Iraqis no longer had such need for the Soviets. I was hoping that in such a situation with all the Arabs turning to us and away from the USSR someone in the Kremlin would have gotten discouraged and said Let's stop pouring so much money and effort down a rat hole. That was the situation we had one week ago. On the whole in the negotiations I think Egypt went further and Israel not as far as I had expected. But our role and the whole strategy we had followed for eighteen months putting us in the key position has been disrupted. Now that the parties are face to face with it they are not so eager for Geneva. A unilateral US effort now would be a mistake would make it look as if we were more anxious than the parties. If they came to us we could think about doing something but there can not be any more shuttles. The pressure on the Arabs is likely to be against cooperating with us. Sadat will have to move toward the other Arabs in order to protect himself and also a bit toward the Soviets and Western Europeans and Geneva. Moreover tensions in the area will build up. [GERALD-FOR] President: I decided to include the Lance and the LGB because I thought they needed it. In retrospect bearing in mind what I believed we were going to do together and what has actually happened we were probably too generous. President: Jim hold off on delivering those high priority items if there is a way to do it.

[JAMES-SCHL] Schlesinger: We have a commitment to deliver the Lance.

[NELSON-ROC] Vice President: I thought they had a commitment too on negotiations.

[WILLIAM-CL] Clements: We can prolong the Lance training in order to delay delivery.

[GERALD-FOR] President: Stay within the guidelines. How you implement it is your business. When we have reassessed then we can proceed. For the moment I would like to look at the four slices of arms we gave them and what we have delivered already.

[JAMES-SCHL] Schlesinger: Haig was here last week complaining about the drawdowns on NATO stocks in Europe. I told him he knew all about it.

[GERALD-FOR] President: I would like to see those four slices. Did we go so far as to increase their offensive capability not only improve their defensive capability? I want to see everything that has been delivered to Israel. I want to be able to show Congress just how much we have done militarily for Israel. Also I would like to see what we have delivered to the Arabs in the way of military hardware.

[GEORGE-BRO] General Brown: There is the question of when the stocks we have drawn down for Israel will be replaced for our own forces. You can use this with Congress.

[GERALD-FOR] President: That would be useful. Get me a list of what we have done since I have been President. If challenged I want the record.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: It would also be valuable to know what we have delivered since November 1973 when our major re-equipment program began.

[GERALD-FOR] President: That will be useful for background but the stress should be on what has happened since I came to office so show where the cut-off is. We have drawn down our own capability.

[WILLIAM-CL] Clements: We have even drawn out of our own stocks.

[GERALD-FOR] President: I want to look at the facts. Bill (Colby) do you want to talk?

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: A. major factor is the increased chance of war. We put out a Special National Intelligence Estimate yesterday. The armies of Egypt Syria and Israel are all in a state of alert and there is a substantial chance of hostilities breaking out either deliberately or by accident at any time in the next few weeks. If it does not happen quickly then there will be negotiations at Geneva and if there is no progress there by early summer there are high odds that Egypt and Syria will launch a coordinated attack and even higher odds that Israel will attack first. Israel probably sees war as inevitable and may decide to hit now. Comparatively they are well off. They can probably beat Egypt and Syria both in 7-10 days.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: We told Asad this was our estimate of how the war would develop not Israel's estimate but our own. Asad told me we did not understand: We learned in 1973 that Israel can not stand pain. We will lose a lot but we will not give up and we will use the strategy of inflicting casualties and fighting an extended war. We will lose territory and men but bleed Israel and draw the Soviets in.

[JAMES-SCHL] Schlesinger: If Israel strikes first they will not behave rationally. They are likely to strike through Lebanon.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: They may be able to hit quickly but the Syrians are determined to hold out.

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: We project 7 000 Israeli killed three times as many as in October 1973. But we believe they can punch through.

[JOSEPH-SIS] Sisco: The Arabs will not stick their necks out. This is a very critical judgment. It can determine the outcome of the war. The Arabs will fight on the defensive and drag it out as long as possible.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: The Arabs think of prolonged war and an early oil embargo.

[JAMES-SCHL] Schlesinger: Before the US resupplies? That would be crazy. We won't stand for it.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: We must think of it. Also our contingency planning needs to assume higher risk-taking by the Soviets.

[GERALD-FOR] President: Did the Soviets go further in 1973 than before?

[JAMES-SCHL] Schlesinger: They threatened the British and French in 1956 with nuclear attack.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Only after we had dissociated ourselves from our allies and told them to pull back.

[JAMES-SCHL] Schlesinger: The Soviets were all bluster.

[WILLIAM-CL] Clements: The priority problem is that Israel may decide their position will worsen so they will preempt. They already had before April 1st enough to preempt and as their situation worsens they could decide to go now. Also as we became more aloof this could aggravate the situation. It could push them to this kind of decision.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: We must weigh many factors. I agree with Bill that if there is no progress by summer there will be war within one year or maybe this year. We have six months to produce something. For Israel to go to war at the known displeasure of the U. S. would be a monumental decision. We must keep the Arabs from becoming too upset but show Israel they can not ignore us. The next time we must be in a position to get results from Israel.

[JAMES-SCHL] Schlesinger: Maybe the word aloof is not a good one. We can say to the Israelis that we have made an honest effort and our well is temporarily dry. Whether it will be temporary or permanent depends on you. We are here.

[GERALD-FOR] President: Rocky what about your talks with Sadat and the Saudis?

[NELSON-ROC] Vice President: Mr. President your thought of sending someone to the funeral of King Feisal and your letters made a deep impression and I believe really helped the Saudis get through a very difficult period. Saudi Arabia wants to follow the policy of cooperation of King Feisal judging from my talks with Khalid and Fahd. I told Fahd we want his advice. He said that Feisal had stood up to Nasser on radicalism in the Arab world when it appeared that Saudi Arabia was all alone but by the time of his death Egypt had come around to seeing that Feisal was right. Fahd said however that unless there is a just equitable and lasting peace within one year --and those are his exact words--the Soviets will move back in the radicals will be reinvigorated and rearmed by the Soviets while the moderates will move away from the US and establish a close relationship with Western Europe. The Europeans have arms they want to sell we have the money to buy and we can learn to fly the planes and drive the tanks. The Arabs will keep building their military strength as long as it takes from the USSR and Western Europe and in time we will crush Israel. That is what Fahd said to me. He is right about the Western Europeans. The French sent their Defense Minister to the funeral with a list of items for sale and models of aircraft and tanks. This offended the Saudis.

[WILLIAM-SI] Simon: Israel might strike first. Is Egypt fully resupplied? I gather they are not and Israel is militarily superior. They won't allow the Arabs to fight a war of attrition. Also if there is too much uncertainty about our support it could lead Israel to conclude it must hit first.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Our problem would be the same if Israel hits soon or later on. Even if Israel destroys the Arab armies we will face the same problems in our relations with the Arabs Western Europeans and Soviets. We would be obliged to step in tell Israel that is enough and impose or try to impose a settlement along the 1967 line. There is a physical limit to what three million people can occupy and sooner or later we will have to stop this process.

[GERALD-FOR] President: Exactly. How many miles of territory and how many cities can Israel occupy?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And would the Soviets stand by while that happened?

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: We think the Soviets are freer to support the Arabs than they have been before. It would take them only a very few days to fly in defensive support such as SAMs and aircraft. Their airborne troops could probably be beaten by the Israelis because they would only be lightly armed but they could reinforce the air defense around Cairo and Damascus and other cities.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: I am not sure Israel would directly attack Soviet troops.

[GEORGE-BRO] Brown: When I was reading the Special National Intelligence Estimate I had the impression of hearing an old record over again. We made a mistake about the Arabs in October 1973. What Sisco had to say is very important. We must keep our minds open.

[JAMES-SCHL] Schlesinger: Israel will certainly win another round.

[GEORGE-BRO] Brown: Israel's army is very good. We know that. But don't count out the Arabs.

[NELSON-ROC] Vice President: Think what another war would mean for us. The OPEC countries would stick together in an oil embargo particularly since the Latin Americans are already unhappy with us. This could cause paralysis of the East Coast of the United States.

[GERALD-FOR] President: I told Morton to put together a contingency plan on what would be likely to happen if there were another oil embargo what measures we can take and what the probable result would be. We need to follow up on this.

[WILLIAM-SI] Simon: I don't believe Venezuela will shut off exports to the U. S.

[NELSON-ROC] Vice President: Venezuela is leading the movement of Latin American solidarity in standing up to the U. S. on economic matters. Would you like to take the risk if you were Governor of New Jersey?

[WILLIAM-CL] Clements: I agree with Nelson.

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: We would have two or three months of grace due to our stockpiles.

[WILLIAM-CL] Clements: There is the geographical dislocation problem. We are just not set up to transfer our production and stocks rapidly enough from one part of the country to another.

[GERALD-FOR] President: I told FEA and others to get some contingency plans ready. I have decided that when Congress comes back on the 9th or 10th I am going to speak to a Joint Session on foreign policy. I am going to lay it on the line Far East Middle East National Security and Defense and other topics. The President has to speak out strongly and positively. Send your suggestions to Brent for incorporation in the speech. We will announce it tomorrow and I will spend a lot of time in California on this. Henry will come out and help. By the time I get back on the 7th we will be in shape for the speech. The American people want to know where they are and Congress needs to know what to do. The State of the Union message had nothing on foreign policy so it has been a long time since a major address on this subject. [At this point the discussion turned to Southeast Asia]

[ROBERT-ING] Deputy Secretary Ingersoll joined the meeting.

[GERALD-FOR] President: Bill what is the situation on the ground in Vietnam?

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: The Vietnamese Government has enough to control the area around Saigon and the Delta for this dry season but they are likely to be defeated in 1976. Thieu tried to extract his troups from the highlands in time but his ploy failed. He was so afraid of leaks to the Communists that he told no one in advance not even his own commanders who were caught by surprise. There was really only one battle. Thieu was aware of the superior comparative strength of the North Vietnamese in the highlands so he wanted to pull out of Pleiku and Kontum. He wanted to fight at Ban Me Thuot but he could not do it. Among other problems his C-130s were sidelined. So the move to the coast became a route instead of an orderly withdrawal. Then they were attacked in Quang Tri and Thieu was indecisive about Hue first he was not going to fight and then he was and then he finally decided not to. This caused the commander of I Corps to become confused and angry. And now the airborne their best troops are being taken out of Danang to Nha Trang and Saigon. Thieu also wants to bring the Marine Division out of the perimeter around Danang. If so Danang will surely fall. Originally Thieu wanted to defend the enclaves like General Gavin.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Colby's estimate indicates that Thieu's pullback was designed to put him into a position to cut his losses and stagger through until 1976. He decided to do this because he was not getting enough support from the U. S. It was due to a lack of spare parts and ammunition. The idea of pulling back was not bad but when the move began the refugees clogged the road and the troops did not know how to move anyway. Thieu was trying to get ready. His estimate and ours was the same; an all-out attack next year would finish him unless he got more support. So he wanted to stagger through this year and hope for a change.

[WILLIAM-CL] Clements: He did not tell us anything at all and did not tell his own commanders.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: The move could only have been carried out by surprise.

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: The refugee figures have fluctuated up and down with the highest point coming after the Tet offensive. Now we are back up to over one million refugees.

[GERALD-FOR] President: Can the Vietnamese be economically self-sufficient in the smaller area?

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: Yes the Delta is the big rice area. This would have been the first year of economic self-sufficiency had it not been for the suddenly deteriorating situation. The refugees are placing a big burden on the government but it is interesting to note that they are all fleeing toward the government. That shows clearly how they really feel about the Communists.

[WILLIAM-CL] Clements: But the army may leave some $200 million in arms and military equipment in Danang alone.

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: And there is some grumbling about Thieu in the army as well as in political circles. We may hear more about this.

[GERALD-FOR] President: You are not optimistic about Danang being held?

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: It should fall within two weeks even if the Marine Division stays instead of being pulled back to protect Saigon.

[GERALD-FOR] President: What about the evacuation of civilians?

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: There have been terrible mob scenes both at the airport where they stormed loading aircraft and at the port where they jammed aboard ships. Some of the military have even shot their way on to the ships. A small number has been loaded but law and order has broken down completely and it is almost impossible.

[ROBERT-ING] Ingersoll: Reportedly 6 000 refugees got off on one ship this morning and another one is loading now.

[GERALD-FOR] President: What are these rumors about Ky coming back?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Ky is a boy scout a flamboyant pop-off; he can not do the job.

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: Chief of Staff Vien and Prime Minister Khiem are possible candidates to replace Thieu.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Thieu has shown himself far and away the most capable of all the Vietnamese leaders I have known since 1965. No one else could do as well. He holds things together. He made a mistake in ordering the withdrawal from the highlands but he had no good choice. We were unable to give him the support he needed.

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: I agree with Henry. No one else is up to Thieu. Khiem would probably be the next best bet but he is some way from being up to Thieu.

[GEORGE-BRO] General Brown: I agree with Colby's estimate about Danang. It will be hard to hold 10 days. We have gotten all the Americans out. A second ship is loading. There are two airfields the main one at Marble Mountain and a small one. There is an ARVN battalion protecting the small one from the mobs and some C-47 flights are getting off. The mobs took the main field and may take the second one.

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: There is little fighting in the Delta and around Saigon. Unless the North Vietnamese move their reserve divisions into the Delta from the North Saigon and the Delta can probably be held militarily but the big problem will come when the stories about Danang start to circulate in Saigon. Concerning Cambodia Lon Nol is going to leave for Indonesia on April first. But there is no hope of talks with the Communists. They will see Lon Nol's departure as weakness and will push harder. The new Communist proposal for a government would leave Sihanouk with no base at all even if he was ostensibly the President.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: The war is now being conducted against Sihanouk. If it were a question of Lon Nol leaving and then our dealing with Sihanouk it would be easy. But the Khmer Rouge want to erase all possible political base for Sihanouk and bring him back only as a front for themselves. The French told us at Martinique that Sihanouk wanted to negotiate but was unable due to the Khmer Rouge.

[WILLIAM-CO] Colby: The Cambodian airlift is suspended. The Communists could make the airfield unusable. The Government is losing ground east of the capital and also down along the river. The wet season starts in late May but the river will not come up until late July and by then it will probably be too late.

[JAMES-SCHL] Schlesinger: We are getting the first reports that the Cambodian troops are beginning to lose their drive. They are worried about U. S. support and losing their commanders. With adequate resupply they would have lasted through the dry season. But the morale is no good. The debate in Congress has hurt them badly. It is likely to collapse in two weeks.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: We have to make an evacuation decision. Ideally from the political viewpoint we should hold on until after your speech and after Congress makes a decision on our aid request. But if we wait it could collapse all at once before we can get our people out. But if we pull out we will surely provoke a collapse. There are about 1100 people of all nationalities to be evacuated. We may need to decide next week.

[GEORGE-BRO] General Brown: The situation has changed. The outlook is bleaker. We need to decide now to take them out or we could have a major problem. There is one brigade of Marines in the Pacific. We could use U. S. forces to take out the residents and try to beat the mob out with helicopters.

[GERALD-FOR] President: How long will it take to get them out?

[GEORGE-BRO] General Brown: If we have to use helicopters downtown it would take one day to get 1200 out. If we have the airfield it would take less time. They can get there on their own. This is a very difficult operation.

[NELSON-ROC] Vice President: The Marines might have to shoot civilians and that would create a huge uproar.

[GEORGE-BRO] General Brown: The mob will be hard to control. We might have to shoot refugees in front of the press.

[GERALD-FOR] President: If you decide to use the airport will you need to clear out the enemy?

[GEORGE-BRO] General Brown: We may need air cover. If there is any firing on our people on the ground at the airport we will attack. We will have aircraft in the air.

[WILLIAM-CL] Clements: We can't tell whether or not the Khmer Rouge will fight us.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: We need a joint estimate about the unravelling in Cambodia. If they can't hold you need a chance to look at the situation. We need an estimate as to how long it can hold so we can decide on whether or not to order fixed wing aircraft in for evacuation.

[NELSON-ROC] Vice President: There is also the symbolism of Lon Nol leaving. This will have a bad effect on morale.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: The Khmer Rouge will negotiate only unconditional surrender. They could get a negotiated settlement anytime but they refuse it. When Lon Nol leaves it will demoralize the country. Long Boret will try to carry on but will fail.

[JAMES-SCHL] Schlesinger: How long do we keep the Americans there after Lon Nol leaves?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: We are pressing them to get out. Lon Nol wanted to stay but we had to press him to get out also to calm the situation.

[GEORGE-BRO] General Brown: We need a decision now on improving our intelligence capability. We can not wait for the Forty Committee General Brown:Mr. President. Will you authorize us to preposition intelligence collection aircraft now for us over North VietNam if we need it?

[GERALD-FOR] President: Yes that is okay.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Mr. President?

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: How are you getting along in your briefings?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well, I've had a--I've had an hour with--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Abrams?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --Abrams. And he's fully aboard, enthusiastically aboard.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: That's been very important.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And he's coming in. And he's leaving tomorrow night. He thinks he needs a day to work with Bunker, and--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --he's full of ideas of how we can do this, technically.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And, you know, how to shift over the air control, and so forth--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah. Yeah. Let me ask a couple of questions--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --and we--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah--?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --I was really very heartened by him. I read him all the provisions on the military side.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Right. What about the govern--What about the political side?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Oh, I haven't told him any of that, but--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --that's no good. I'm using that office as a club, by telling them what their old proposals were.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah. I see.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: He'll go along with the political side. There's no question on that.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Um-hmm.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: The political side is a smashing victory. I mean there's no--there will be no one who will question the political side.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: [unclear] the only problem I see there is--from our standpoint is--which I want to be sure we're adequately warned on is--is the use of the word """"coalition"""" in any--any form, shape, whatever.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: It's not mentioned.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Oh, I know it isn't in that. But I meant in terms of the--of what the press says, what the pub[lic]--what is said by either side, and so forth. The--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: No, we can't--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: The point being--the point being--I don't mean what the other side says. But we say--the point being that, once that is said, then the indication will be by our--our critics that, well, that we could have gotten this four years ago. You see? The coalition business. That's why the coalition thing has got to be, has got to be in your own briefing. If we come to a briefing it's got to be very, very tough. This is not a coalition government under any circumstances--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: No, that's not--nothing changes anyway. Right? The only thing that happens immediately on the political side is the negotiations between Thieu and the others.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: I understand that. I understand that there's a Council of National Concord,2 but they're going to--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Yeah, but it doesn't come into being--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Right.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --until Thieu has negotiated it with the other side.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Right. And, basically, that is not a government, either. But the point is--right?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Right. Oh, right.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah. But the point that I make is that, as you can see, that is the point that has to be very carefully--we've got to be straight-arming him on that issue so that we don't run into any problem there.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Right.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Right.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: With that, I am confident that the political side is in excellent shape. I mean, in fact, there is nobody in this country who could imagine that we could get this political settlement.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah. Well, that's my feeling. That's my feeling. That's my feeling.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: It's the thinnest face-saver.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Um-hmm. Um-hmm. Um-hmm. With regard to the questions you'd raised earlier with Bob,3 let me just run over it briefly, because I made a few--I had a few thoughts on it last night. First, to keep it all in perspective, we should understand that, that the major consideration should be the making of a settlement.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Right.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: The making of a settlement is not going to hurt us in the election, and it isn't going to help us significantly. You know, who can tell? But the main point is what could hurt, really, is to go down the road and then--and then fail.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Right.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: That is why I think even before going to Saigon,4 I would--I think we have to be fairly, fairly sure that--that, well, not fairly sure, but at least have a pretty good chance of making it go. If you go to Saigon, and it doesn't go, of course, then--I mean, you can't even really consider going to Hanoi, because if you do, it escalates it to a point where we just couldn't, we just couldn't--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: I agree.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: --stand it. But if you could go to--and I don't know, but what--you think Abrams can do a little softening up before you get there--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: No.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: --that's the point.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: No, no. But he and Bunker can start analyzing. You see, after we get Thieu's agreement--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --there'll have to be a hell of a lot of work done.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And we could then focus Thieu not on how he's going to stonewall the agreement, but how is he going to shift certain categories of things, who is going to take them over, and so forth.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Right. Right. Right. What does Bunker think? What's his view about whether--well, he doesn't know about the political thing is, but what is his view about Thieu's reaction to this?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: I haven't checked on that with him yet, but we have--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: At least you have Bunker's reaction. I don't mean Bunker's. I don't mean that--I meant Abrams's view.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well, Abrams says it's hard to predict.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: He thinks that Thieu ought to accept this, that this is a great opportunity for him.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Right.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: He's enthusiastic.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Right. Right.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And on the political side, we're in--I assure you, Mr. President, there's no sophisticate who will not see that this is the thinnest form of face-saver for the other--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Right. Right.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Thieu stays, there's no coalition government, the negotiations start. Then they form a sort of a half-ass committee.5

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: I know.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: If it ever comes into being.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: That's right. Right.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: But--So, we've had another little message from theNorth Vietnamese--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Is that right? Yeah?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --last night, screaming about the five changes I've given them.6

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: But if--the thing could fall apart on Tuesday.7

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: In that case, of course, I come back from Paris.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Right.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: The thing could fall apart in Saigon. In that case, I come back from Saigon. I agree completely that I shouldn't--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: You can't escalate that that high, because otherwise we're--then we're then where the fat's in the fire, and it'll appear as if Thieu is with the people--the person that torpedoed it.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: I agree.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah. And I, incidentally, the--on the other side, I don't--there need be no concern about the political effect. We just can't think in the terms of the fact: """"Well, gee whiz, it'd be better not to have this politically."""" Sure, it's risky. We don't need it. We're going to win without it, and very heavily. But the point is that you've got to take a risk to get the damned war over. And if there's more, if there is--if this is the best settlement we can get--which I think it is--and if this is the best time, when the forces will be the strongest to get it, then the thing to do is to push it and get it. That's my attitude.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Right.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: You see?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Right.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: We're in this. We're in that situation where, where we've just got to say what it really comes down to, Henry, is the merit of the settlement. If it's the right settlement, and this is the best time, do it now.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: I would--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: If it's the right settlement, and we should do it at a later time, put it off later. The--as far as what--as the election is concerned, don't be bothered with it, either way. There's only--there's only one thing on the election, as I say, and it would not be fatal, and that would be to have either Thieu or the North Vietnamese to blow it.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Of course, if we can--one risk we run is the one point that Mel made to me was, when I went into all the refinements we were getting, he said: """"Listen, you have to face one thing. If they offer us this deal publicly--""""

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: """"--we'll be forced to accept it, without refinements.""""
